The Best Books in (and on) Translation We Read in 2025
By Words Without Borders
13 staff members, 11 countries, 9 languages: The WWB team recommends our favorite books in translation from 2025.
December 11, 2025
Chile Denmark France Georgia Hong Kong Iraq Italy Palestine Spain Turkey United States Uzbekistan Reading Lists
I’d memorized Cesare Pavese’s poem “The Cats Will Know” when I was nineteen and still getting used to hostel life in Delhi (my friends named our collective poetry chapbook after it too), and later, in my mid-twenties, when I was an international student in the UK, perpetually walking through woods, museums, and quaint neighborhoods to shake off any homesickness, I’d keep borrowing Pavese’s Disaffections (tr. Geoffrey Brock) from the library, feeling like his poems were my map and talisman. So, a few months ago, when my friend and I decided to read Tezer Özlü’s autofictional Journey to the Edge of Life for our two-person book club, I knew I’d get pulled into that brooding mood again, which can be somewhat addictive, especially in early winter, only to realize pleasantly that one of the themes that Özlü explores in the novel is indeed the relationship between memory, solitude, recall, and reading literature. The narrative unravels slowly, like a long walk through new and sometimes alienating European cities, as the narrator goes in search of her literary soulmate, Cesare Pavese, and also encounters places and people haunted by other writers like Kafka and Svevo. The plot expands like a mysterious patch of water, mixing the past with the present and absorbing bits of other genres as it grows, including poems and playlike dialogue. The novel’s loitering sentences and dreamy temporal shifts have been beautifully translated from the Turkish by Maureen Freely (who has also written an engaging introduction and a translator’s note). We’d read Thuận ’s Chinatown (tr. Nguyễn An Lý) the previous month, and my friend and I loved discussing the echoes we could hear within the two novels ( Chinatown ’s narrator, also an Asian woman navigating European cities, is obsessed with Marguerite Duras). Özlü’s narrator rejects borders and nationalities and writes: “I am not a citizen. No country or class can claim me.” What is also fascinating is that Özlü first wrote the novel in German and then rewrote it in Turkish, and these kinds of bilingual rewritings are supremely interesting to me, prompting musings on geographies, histories, and identities of people and places. I was also inspired to revisit another great read from this year: Yoko Tawada’s Exophony (tr. Lisa Hofmann-Kuroda), in which the author writes: “Maybe what I really want is not to be a writer of this or that language in particular, but to fall into the poetic ravine between them.”
—Sohini Basak, Poetry Editor
When done well, politically charged poetry can leave its impact the way few other words can. That’s what makes Bodies Found in Various Places: The Selected Poems of Elvira Hernández , translated by Daniel Borzutzky and Alec Schumacher, such an essential read for me this year. Like Pedro Lemebel’s essay collection A Last Supper of Queer Apostles , this is a collection of searing work that pushes back against the authoritarian status quo of Pinochet-era Chile. And when you read lines like “Your skeleton is a devoured fish whose bones / are pulled out of their teeth,” from “TearfaLL,” it’s often accompanied by a visceral chill at its utterly tactile imagery.
—Tobias Carroll, Watchlist Editor
Claire Baglin’s On the Clock , translated by Jordan Stump, drops the reader directly into the two narrative strands that make up the novel: a young woman’s summer of work in a fast-food chain restaurant, and her father’s life of working in a car-parts factory while raising his family. We learn about the narrator and her family in this novel written almost entirely in scene; like many of us, these characters go to work, come home, and try to “clock out” for one or two vacations a year. Stump’s translation of Baglin is taut, and tension grows as we witness the development of both the father’s and daughter’s careers. We do not merely dedicate our bodies to work (of which the novel shows the extremes, in a few harrowing scenes); we also dedicate—and risk losing—our minds. “When Jérôme fixes things he always wounds himself before he succeeds, as if the brokenness had to pass from the object to his body before it can disappear,” Baglin and Stump write. With realism at turns humorous and grim, On the Clock reminds us how much we sacrifice to make a living, and what we must try to preserve, at all costs. I love reading debut novels because they contain so much potential for future enjoyment; after inhaling On the Clock in a few days this summer, I’m eagerly awaiting Baglin’s next work.
—Emma Deshpande, 2025–26 Education Fellow
Paco Cerdà’s The Pawn, translated from Spanish by Kevin Gerry Dunn, sets a 1962 match between Bobby Fischer and the first Spanish grandmaster, Arturito Pomar, against the political anxieties of the time. Cerdà finds pawns (“those employed to advance the intentions of another”) everywhere, applying the chess metaphor across the board to reveal a universe of gambits. Chockablock with chess lore and Cold War history and grounded in the quotidian oppression of the Franco era, the book reads like a thriller, with a tone of defeat and moral cowardice reminiscent of the best of le Carré. In a jaw-dropping afterword, Cerdà declares that “not a single detail or word of dialogue [comes] from the author’s imagination,” and the seven pages of sources that follow demonstrate the range and breadth of his research. (Dunn, of course, then had to recreate that material in English, which brings to mind the line about Ginger Rogers doing everything Fred Astaire did, plus backward and in high heels.)
—Susan Harris, Editorial Director
Last month in Tucson, Michelle Mirabella pressed her translation of The Cracks We Bear by Chilean author Catalina Infante into my hands, and am I ever glad she did. This slim, electric novella pairs a story of new motherhood with an exploration of grief and exile. As the narrator, Laura, struggles with the reduction of her own identity in the early days of motherhood, she also grapples with the limited way she knew her own late mother. In chapters that alternate between the present and her strained memories, Laura goes in search of a more multifaceted understanding, both of her mother and of herself. The Cracks We Bear joins the ranks of several titles about early motherhood published in translation or by translators in recent years. Linea Nigra by Jazmina Barrera, translated by Christina MacSweeney; In Vitro by Isabel Zapata, translated by Robin Myers; and The Long Form by Kate Briggs have been among my favorites. The Cracks We Bear is a debut for both Mirabella and Infante; what a firecracker start to their careers.
—Elisabeth Jaquette, Executive Director
Hamid Ismailov’s We Computers , translated by Shelley Fairweather-Vega, offers a consideration of artificial intelligence so casual that it feels markedly surreal in this feverish moment of development and heightened concern over the technology. This feeling aligns with the novel’s interest in the nebulous boundaries between making, doing, and being, and its questions surrounding authorship and the legacy of poetry. Formally, the book is complex, with an unreliable AI narrator and layer upon layer of translation and speculation between versions of the Persian poetry that is its subject and all of its multilingual mediators—the protagonist and peer translators, the aforementioned narrator. At what point in the lifespan of a work of art do its (re)interpretations become part of the work? Ismailov asks the reader to suspend judgment and observe these lyrical (human and nonhuman) collaborations across time, and the inevitable mistakes that come with them. For technoskeptic poetry readers like myself, We Computers is a simultaneously challenging and deeply pleasurable read.
—Sophia Marisa Lucas, Digital Manager
For all its grim subject matter—it begins with a teacher disappearing deep into the woods, after hearing the news that her student has jumped out of a window and taken her own life— Dear Teacher surprised me by being a gentle (and often funny) book. It is in part a reconstruction of a family story that the author, Maddalena Vaglio Tanet, recalls hearing vague fragments of as a child, and later researched for the book, speaking to witnesses and combing through newspapers. What I liked was how it breathed life into the bare bones of a story that could have stayed another headline, imagining with tenderness how people’s lives unravel or simply carry on after a cataclysmic event. A ten-year-old boy begins visiting the teacher where she is hiding, bringing her food so she survives. They talk about school, mothers, dogs, and books, and an unlikely friendship begins to take off. The big worries of a small kid, the desperation of a woman neck-deep in a crisis, the regular lives of the people in the town: As the novel shuttles between these perspectives, it contemplates, with flecks of humor and lyricism that the translation captures subtly, what makes people want to walk away from their lives and the connections that may make them want to come back.
—Maya Palit, Books Editor
I’m certainly not the first person to say this, but I have found myself captivated by Solvej Balle’s On the Calculation of Volume novels, the third of which was published in English last month (tr. by Sophia Hersi Smith and Jennifer Russell). I won’t give any spoilers here, and in fact very little “happens,” plotwise, as we follow protagonist Tara Selter through her endlessly repeating November 18th—from the discovery that she is trapped in a time loop through her attempts to both escape and cope with her situation. But these are books of immense depth and mournfulness: Balle has considered every detail of Tara’s world and state of mind, and she takes us there, to the bizarre places our thoughts go, the slightly unhinged behaviors that crop up, when we’ve spent too much time alone. In Book III, for instance, Tara decides to leave Germany solely because the sounds she hears there have begun to feel “wrong”— a choice that strikes me as both nonsensical and intuitively true. Admirably, Balle takes her time with these books, earning each revelation and allowing new questions about the implications of November 18th to unfold organically (I’m haunted, for example, by the knowledge that Tara will at some point age beyond recognition for Thomas). I also have to applaud the seamless translator handoff from Barbara J. Haveland to Sophia Hersi Smith and Jennifer Russell: With Book III, the new duo have done an impressive job of maintaining the voice Haveland crafted for Books I and II. The fourth book promises new developments for Tara, but in the meantime, the first three are available to sit with and to savor.
—Nina Perrotta, Senior Editor and Development Manager
I’m probably a little biased because I’ve always loved the City Lights Pocket Poets series, but this collection really resonated with me. Rabah leans fully into imagery, and it shows; so many of these poems feel surreal, heartbreaking, and quietly wistful. He has a way of finding beauty in small, everyday moments, and that sensitivity gives the entire collection a vivid, lingering quality. There are so many great poems in this collection, but my favorites are “Water Thirsty For Water” and “The Flattery of Air.”
—Molly Ripatti, Social Media Coordinator
Suzanne Jill Levine’s Unfaithful offers a front-row seat to the Boom—the so-called explosion onto the 1960s and ‘70s anglophone literary scene by Latin American writers including Julio Cortázar (AR) and Carlos Fuentes (MX), both of whom number among the authors whose work she translated. If ever anyone was in the right place at the right time, Levine was, and her fast-paced (and sometimes racy!) memoir details her work and relationships with many of these great writers. Far more than an amanuensis, in this memoir Levine proves that a translator is a writer’s closest reader, and that she is very much a writer herself. Indispensable for lovers of Latin American literature.
Bonus! The scene in which Pablo Neruda helps her cut up a mango during a dinner party first appeared in WWB, and for a taste (haha!) of Unfaithful you can read it here .
—Samantha Schnee, Founding Editor and Chairman of the Board
Abu Zayd al-Ansari’s The Book of Rain —originally composed in ninth-century Basra and conscientiously shepherded into English this year by David Larsen with an expert hand—bowled me over for its fine-grained attunement to nuances of cloud-shape, river-flow, and thunder-rumble. Why haven’t our meteorological forecasts begun adopting the Frisk, the Dribble, or—even better—the Beetle-Brow to warn us of the icky varieties of spattering precipitation that descend upon the unsheltered heads of New York City’s denizens? As usual, the ancient Arabs were far ahead of the curve; one of the oldest surviving pre-Islamic poems by the famous Imru’ al-Qays likens lightning to the play of “fluorescent hands,” the flicker of a monk’s lamp. Peruse at leisure Larsen’s delightful index—longer than al-Ansari’s actual text and appended to its end—of sundry annotations, philological musings, and witty anecdotes from the classical Arabic archive for appetizing tidbits on horse foreheads and angel cries. This mass of footnotes, a quasi-Nabokovian tic, structurally mirrors and pays tribute to the Arabic exegetical tradition, where the proliferating allusions in the commentary often overwhelmed the original material in a deluge of erudition. I thought equally of Lisa Robertson’s magnificently strange The Weather , collaged from BBC shipping forecasts, Romantic poetry, and Constable’s cloud sketches: “The rain has loosened; we engage our imagination. The sentence opens inexpensively; we imagine its silence.”
As much a craft manual, a feat of translation, and a formally daring experiment in our epoch of climate apocalypse as it is a lexicographical treatise and celestial history, The Book of Rain marvelously returns us to the childlike wonder of discovering new names for our world. Cataclysmic or quotidian, impersonal or fallaciously pathetic, the weather in al-Ansari’s eyes takes on a multitude of guises for every readerly disposition. How thrilling that this text is a drop in the foamy crest of Wave Books, a publisher whose avant-garde cred spans the likes of Don Mee Choi and Mary Ruefle. The time (and tide) is ripe, perhaps, for a resurgence of classical Arabic literature in uncannily clairvoyant, new forms. We still have much to learn from how it sought, and found, poetics peeking through each crevice of sky.
—Alex Tan, 2025–26 Editorial Fellow
I’m still thinking about Hon Lai Chu’s Mending Bodies , translated by Jacqueline Leung. This moody, allegorical book imagines an economically depressed city whose government passes a Conjoinment Act, an initiative that encourages residents to surgically attach themselves to another person in exchange for social and financial benefits. Choosing your other half isn’t so much a question of love as it is one of corporeal compatibility—mismatched bodies can reject one another after surgery like transplanted organs—and participants in the program soon learn that adapting to a shared body is equally taxing on the mind. Narrated by a university student researching conjoinment for her dissertation, the novel includes case studies from the protagonist’s academic work that tease out the characters’ feelings of alienation. What she uncovers through her schoolwork and her own lived experience is a society racked with insomnia, dysphoria, and fractured selves. Leung’s translation is both poetic and visceral, and Hon imagines a world so suffocating I can’t quite shake it off.
—Maggie Vlietstra, Education Program Manager
I could not put The Lack of Light down, but not because, as many other reviewers claim, of its closeness to Elena Ferrante’s work. To me, The Lack of Light is totally singular. The novel is indeed anchored in the intimate yet fraught relationships of a group of four neighborhood friends who grow apart, then are pulled back together at one of the friends’ photography retrospectives, but it skillfully uses these relationships, Dina’s photography, and Keto’s interiority to bring Tbilisi, pre- and post-civil war, to life. Though many themes and scenes bear similarities to other work from former Soviet member countries, Haratischwili effortlessly eschews their stereotypes, and even the most heart-rending or uplifting scenes refuse easy sentimentality. The joint translation by Charlotte Collins and Ruth Martin is lush and exquisite, to the point where I forced myself to slow down (as much as it is a page-turner) so that I could linger on the prose longer. It’s my new must-read epic novel.
—Anna Claire Weber, Marketing and Communications Manager

I’m still thinking about Hon Lai Chu’s Mending Bodies , translated by Jacqueline Leung. This moody, allegorical book imagines an economically depressed city whose government passes a Conjoinment Act, an initiative that encourages residents to surgically attach themselves to another person in exchange for social and financial benefits. Choosing your other half isn’t so much a question of love as it is one of corporeal compatibility—mismatched bodies can reject one another after surgery like transplanted organs—and participants in the program soon learn that adapting to a shared body is equally taxing on the mind. Narrated by a university student researching conjoinment for her dissertation, the novel includes case studies from the protagonist’s academic work that tease out the characters’ feelings of alienation. What she uncovers through her schoolwork and her own lived experience is a society racked with insomnia, dysphoria, and fractured selves. Leung’s translation is both poetic and visceral, and Hon imagines a world so suffocating I can’t quite shake it off.
—Maggie Vlietstra, Education Program Manager
I could not put The Lack of Light down, but not because, as many other reviewers claim, of its closeness to Elena Ferrante’s work. To me, The Lack of Light is totally singular. The novel is indeed anchored in the intimate yet fraught relationships of a group of four neighborhood friends who grow apart, then are pulled back together at one of the friends’ photography retrospectives, but it skillfully uses these relationships, Dina’s photography, and Keto’s interiority to bring Tbilisi, pre- and post-civil war, to life. Though many themes and scenes bear similarities to other work from former Soviet member countries, Haratischwili effortlessly eschews their stereotypes, and even the most heart-rending or uplifting scenes refuse easy sentimentality. The joint translation by Charlotte Collins and Ruth Martin is lush and exquisite, to the point where I forced myself to slow down (as much as it is a page-turner) so that I could linger on the prose longer. It’s my new must-read epic novel.
—Anna Claire Weber, Marketing and Communications Manager
